article.title: To catch a king
glossary: * Presbyterianism: part of the reformed Protestant religion
* cherub: an image of angelic children used in paintings

items.sentence_raw: Charles Spencer's latest book, To Catch a King, tells us the story of the hunt for King Charles II in the six weeks after his resounding defeat at the Battle of Worcester in September 1651.
items.explain: Q36: The first paragraph explains the events from his father's death to the battle that forced Charles to flee — this is the **'circumstances leading to Charles II's escape'**. So the answer is **B**.

items.sentence_raw: And what a story it is.

After his father was executed by the Parliamentarians in 1649, the young Charles II sacrificed one of the very principles his father had died for and did a deal with the Scots, thereby accepting Presbyterianism* as the national religion in return for being crowned King of Scots.
items.explain:
Q27: The passage says Charles II *'did a deal with the Scots'* — a **'deal'** here means a **'strategic alliance'**. So the answer is **H**.

Q28: The passage says Charles II *'sacrificed one of the very principles his father had died for'* — a **'principle'** someone dies for is a deep **'religious conviction'**. So the answer is **J**.

items.sentence_raw: His arrival in Edinburgh prompted the English Parliamentary army to invade Scotland in a pre-emptive strike.
This was followed by a Scottish invasion of England.
The two sides finally faced one another at Worcester in the west of England in 1651.

After being comprehensively defeated on the meadows outside the city by the Parliamentarian army, the 21-year-old king found himself the subject of a national manhunt, with a huge sum offered for his capture.
items.explain:
Q29: The passage says Charles was *'comprehensively defeated'* at Worcester — **'comprehensively defeated'** means a **'decisive victory'** for the other side. So the answer is **F**.

Q30: The passage says *'a huge sum offered for his capture'* — a **'huge sum'** offered for catching someone is a **'large reward'**. So the answer is **B**.

items.sentence_raw: Over the following six weeks he managed, through a series of heart-poundingly close escapes, to evade the Parliamentarians before seeking refuge in France.
items.explain: Q31: The passage says Charles escaped by *'seeking refuge in France'* — **'refuge'** means a place of **'relative safety'**. So the answer is **D**.

items.sentence_raw: For the next nine years, the penniless and defeated Charles wandered around Europe with only a small group of loyal supporters.
Years later, after his restoration as king, the 50-year-old Charles II requested a meeting with the writer and diarist Samuel Pepys.
His intention when asking Pepys to commit his story to paper was to ensure that this most extraordinary episode was never forgotten.
Over two three-hour sittings, the king related to him in great detail his personal recollections of the six weeks he had spent as a fugitive.
items.explain: Q33: The passage says Charles told his story *'in great detail'* over two long sittings — **'great detail'** is the opposite of **'lacked sufficient detail'**. So the answer is **NO**.

items.sentence_raw: As the king and secretary settled down (a scene that is surely a gift for a future scriptwriter), Charles commenced his story: "After the battle was so absolutely lost as to be beyond hope of recovery, I began to think of the best way of saving myself."
items.explain: Q34: The passage quotes Charles saying he thought of escape *'After the battle was so absolutely lost'* — this means he planned **after** the defeat, not **'before the battle'**. So the answer is **NO**.

items.sentence_raw: One of the joys of Spencer's book, a result not least of its use of Charles II's own narrative as well as those of his supporters, is just how close the reader gets to the action.
items.explain: Q35: The passage calls Charles's own story *'One of the joys of Spencer's book'* — a **'joy'** is a **'positive aspect'**. So the answer is **YES**.

items.sentence_raw: The day-by-day retelling of the fugitives' doings provides delicious details: the cutting of the king's long hair with agricultural shears, the use of walnut leaves to dye his pale skin, and the day Charles spent lying on a branch of the great oak tree in Boscobel Wood as the Parliamentary soldiers scoured the forest floor below.
items.explain: Q37: The passage says the *'day-by-day retelling'* gives *'delicious details'* like cutting hair and hiding in a tree — these examples **'illustrate how the events are brought to life'**. So the answer is **C**.

items.sentence_raw: Spencer draws out both the humour - such as the preposterous refusal of Charles's friend Henry Wilmot to adopt disguise on the grounds that it was beneath his dignity - and the emotional tension when the secret of the king's presence was cautiously revealed to his supporters.

Charles's adventures after losing the Battle of Worcester hide the uncomfortable truth that whilst almost everyone in England had been appalled by the execution of his father, they had not welcomed the arrival of his son with the Scots army, but had instead firmly bolted their doors.
This was partly because he rode at the head of what looked like a foreign invasion force and partly because, after almost a decade of civil war, people were desperate to avoid it beginning again.
This makes it all the more interesting that Charles II himself loved the story so much ever after.
As well as retelling it to anyone who would listen, causing eyerolling among courtiers, he set in train a series of initiatives to memorialise it.
There was to be a new order of chivalry, the Knights of the Royal Oak.
A series of enormous oil paintings depicting the episode were produced, including a two-metre-wide canvas of Boscobel Wood and a set of six similarly enormous paintings of the king on the run.
In 1660, Charles II commissioned the artist John Michael Wright to paint a flying squadron of cherubs* carrying an oak tree to the heavens on the ceiling of his bedchamber.
It is hard to imagine many other kings marking the lowest point in their life so enthusiastically, or indeed pulling off such an escape in the first place.
items.explain: Q38: The passage says it is hard to imagine other kings *'marking the lowest point in their life so enthusiastically'* — this means Charles **'chose to celebrate what was essentially a defeat'**. So the answer is **A**.

items.sentence_raw: Charles Spencer is the perfect person to pass the story on to a new generation.
His pacey, readable prose steers deftly clear of modern idioms and elegantly brings to life the details of the great tale.

He has even-handed sympathy for both the fugitive king and the fierce republican regime that hunted him, and he succeeds in his desire to explore far more of the background of the story than previous books on the subject have done.
items.explain: Q39: The passage says Spencer has *'even-handed sympathy for both the fugitive king and the fierce republican regime'* — **'even-handed'** means **'unbiased'**. So the answer is **B**.

items.sentence_raw: Indeed, the opening third of the book is about how Charles II found himself at Worcester in the first place, which for some will be reason alone to read To Catch a King.
The tantalising question left, in the end, is that of what it all meant.
Would Charles II have been a different king had these six weeks never happened?
The days and nights spent in hiding must have affected him in some way.
Did the need to assume disguises, to survive on wit and charm alone, to use trickery and subterfuge to escape from tight corners help form him?
This is the one area where the book doesn't quite hit the mark.
items.explain: Q40: The passage says the book *'doesn't quite hit the mark'* because it fails to show if the escape changed Charles — this means it **'fails to address whether experiences had a lasting influence'**. So the answer is **D**.

items.sentence_raw: Instead its depiction of Charles II in his final years as an ineffective, pleasure-loving monarch doesn't do justice to the man (neither is it accurate), or to the complexity of his character.
items.explain: Q40: The passage says the book *'doesn't quite hit the mark'* because it fails to show if the escape changed Charles — this means it **'fails to address whether experiences had a lasting influence'**. So the answer is **D**.

items.sentence_raw: But this one niggle aside, To Catch a King is an excellent read, and those who come to it knowing little of the famous tale will find they have a treat in store.

subtitles: Anna Keay reviews Charles Spencer's book about the hunt for King Charles II during the English Civil War of the seventeenth century

orphan_explain_map.32: Q32: The passage says Charles asked Pepys to write his story, but it never mentions why he chose Pepys — it says nothing about **'trustworthy'**. ***NOT GIVEN is not the same as FALSE*** — so the answer is **NOT GIVEN**.
